title: Discourses close
hookLine: forty lessons from a blunt, kind teacher who was once a slave

cards: There's a kind of teacher who is hard on a student and obviously on their side. The one who hands back the paper covered in red ink, then stays after class to go through it line by line.

The thank-you, if it comes, sometimes comes years later. For more than forty days we've sat in a classroom in Nicopolis with a teacher like that. Today we stand up from the bench, look back at the room, and say goodbye.

teach.b: Epictetus had been enslaved, walked with a lame leg, and in his own talks calls himself a lame old man. He taught at Nicopolis, on the Greek coast. He wrote nothing.
What we have, his student Arrian took down: four books of talks, the Discourses. Arrian says in his preface that he tried to keep the teacher's own words, as notes for himself. The voice is blunt.
He mocks, teases, calls his students lazy and their excuses silly. He'll press a father who ran from his sick daughter's bedside on whether that was really love.

teach.h: BLUNT AND KIND, LIKE A COACH.
teach.b: And he's kind the way a good coach is kind: he won't let you be less than you could be. Look at what we carried out of the room: the gift of use, and not even Zeus can take your choice. Money-changer.
Unhindered. Alone, not lonely, a scout, in its season, kosmopolitēs, free is wanting rightly, nothing to take, my post, peace of mind, and yesterday, attention.
One idea turned forty ways: some things are ours and some aren't, and freedom lives on the side that's ours. Tomorrow a very different Stoic picks up the thread.
Seneca was rich, powerful and close to an emperor, the opposite of a freed slave teaching on the coast, and late in life he wrote letters to a friend. Same porch, new voice.

how: Some readers of Epictetus reread the Discourses over many years, keeping a few lines close, and some write back to him in journals as if to a teacher.

o: a wealthy Stoic who wrote letters to a friend in Sicily
a freed slave and teacher whose talks Arrian wrote down
a Roman emperor who wrote private notes on Stoic life

p: the school on the Greek coast
the next voice on the porch

s: he wrote nothing; his student Arrian took the talks down.
Epictetus speaks of himself as lame and old
in the Discourses he calls himself a lame old man.
Epictetus was gentle and never teased his students
he was blunt, mocking even, and kind the way a good coach is kind.

games.q: a visiting official tells Epictetus he ran from his sick little daughter's bedside because he loved her too much to watch. what does Epictetus do?
o: asks whether that was really love, and presses him to think it through.
tells him to stop coming to class.
games.why: in book one he questions the father until it's clear the leaving came from his own judgment, not from love: blunt, and meant to help.

practice: Picture Epictetus on his bench in Nicopolis, an old man with a stick, students crowding the room, and write him one line: what you'll keep, an argument you still want to have, or just thank you.
Read it back once, slowly, and let it stand. If a teacher from your own life comes to mind, let them have a line too.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus. The freed slave and blunt, kind teacher whose talks his student Arrian wrote down, as we close more than forty days with him.

orig.note: Greek: the teacher's name, as his student Arrian wrote it.

carryVoice: Your line: thank you, teacher. For the red ink, and for staying after class. Goodbye for now, Nicopolis.
